formation.title: The Birth of Mexico
formation.text:
A new nation rises from the ashes of three centuries of colonial rule. The land that was once New Spain (its silver mines, its haciendas, its cathedrals, its peoples of a hundred origins) must now find its own path. Two visions compete for the soul of the new republic. The conservatives look to the Plan de Iguala and its Three Guarantees: the primacy of the Catholic faith, absolute independence from Spain, and the union of all peoples regardless of origin, an orderly transition led by the army and the church. The liberals invoke the Grito de Dolores, the midnight cry of Father Hidalgo that launched a decade of popular revolution, a Mexico built on the sovereignty of the common people, where colonial privileges are swept away and a new republican order rises from below.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Religion, Independence, Union: the Three Guarantees shall be our foundation.

modifiers.name: Three Guarantees
modifiers.text: The Plan de Iguala's three sacred pillars (Religion, Independence, and Union) bind the diverse peoples of Mexico into a single nation under the banner of order and tradition.

options.text: The Cry of Dolores echoes still: the people's revolution continues!

modifiers.name: Cry of Dolores
modifiers.text: The revolutionary spirit of Hidalgo and Morelos lives on. Mexico is a nation forged in popular uprising, where the people's sovereignty transcends the old colonial order.

advances.name: Encomienda System
advances.text: The encomienda grants Spanish settlers the right to extract labor and tribute from indigenous communities, establishing the foundations of colonial agriculture and mining.

advances.name: Silver Mining Revolution
advances.text:
The development of mercury amalgamation transforms silver extraction, making Mexico the world's largest silver producer and its currency the first global medium of exchange.

Available in: Hacienda Grande

event.title: The Silver Revolution
event.text: In the mines of Zacatecas, a breakthrough in metallurgy is transforming the colonial economy. Bartolome de Medina has developed the patio process, mercury amalgamation applied on an industrial scale, which allows silver to be extracted from ores that were previously too poor to work. The impact is staggering. Silver production explodes, and Mexican pesos begin circulating across the globe, from the markets of Seville to the silk shops of Manila, from the counting houses of Amsterdam to the tea houses of Canton. New Spain becomes the engine of the world's first truly global economy, and the silver peso becomes the world's first international currency.

options.text: Mexican silver shall flow to every corner of the world.

advances.name: Cochineal Trade
advances.text: Cochineal dye from the nopal cactus becomes Mexico's second most valuable export, producing vivid crimson that colors the robes of European monarchs and cardinals.

advances.name: Viceregal Administration
advances.text: The audiencia, the viceroy, and the Real Hacienda form the institutional backbone of New Spain, governing a territory stretching from Central America to the Philippines.

advances.name: Colegio Tradition
advances.text: The founding of colleges and the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico creates a distinctive intellectual tradition blending European scholasticism with New World experience.

advances.name: Hacienda System
advances.text: Great agricultural estates combine farming, ranching, and sometimes mining to feed the colonial economy, becoming the dominant institution of rural Mexico.

advances.name: Casta Society
advances.text: The complex racial taxonomy of colonial Mexico (Spaniard, creole, mestizo, mulatto, and dozens of other categories) paradoxically creates a society of remarkable cultural fluidity and synthesis.

advances.name: Silver Peso
advances.text: The Mexican peso de ocho, the piece of eight, becomes the world's first global currency, accepted from Canton to Constantinople.

advances.name: Manila Galleon Trade
advances.text: The nao de China connects Acapulco to Manila, carrying Mexican silver to Asia and returning with silk, spices, and porcelain in the world's first transpacific trade route.

advances.name: Presidio Line
advances.text: A chain of fortified garrisons stretches across the northern frontier, defending settled territory against Comanche, Apache, and other indigenous raiders.

advances.name: Soldados de Cuera
advances.text: The leather-armored dragoons of the frontier presidios are a uniquely Mexican military tradition, cavalry armed with lance, shield, and musket, adapted to the harsh conditions of the northern borderlands.

advances.name: Mexican Baroque
advances.text: The ultra-ornate Churrigueresque style blends Spanish Baroque with indigenous artistic traditions, creating cathedrals and public buildings that embody the mestizo soul of Mexico.

advances.name: Bourbon Reforms
advances.text: The Bourbon dynasty's sweeping administrative reforms (the intendancy system, trade liberalization, military professionalization) modernize New Spain but sow the seeds of creole discontent.

event.title: The Bourbon Reforms
event.text: The Bourbon dynasty has brought sweeping changes to the administration of New Spain. The old Habsburg system of indirect rule through local elites and church intermediaries is being replaced by a rationalized bureaucracy designed to extract more revenue and tighten metropolitan control. The intendancy system replaces the patchwork of corregidores and alcaldes mayores with professional administrators. Restrictions on colonial trade are being loosened. The military is being professionalized. These reforms will strengthen the state, but they also risk alienating the creole elites who have long enjoyed autonomy under the old system. The question is whether to embrace centralization fully or to focus the reforms on commercial expansion.

options.text: Centralize the administration: efficiency demands order.

modifiers.name: Intendancy System
modifiers.text: The Bourbon administrative reforms have centralized governance through the intendancy system, replacing the old alcalde mayor network with professional administrators who answer directly to the crown.

options.text: Open the ports: prosperity flows through free commerce.

modifiers.name: Free Commerce Decree
modifiers.text: The liberalization of colonial trade regulations has opened new ports and commercial routes, breaking the old monopoly system and allowing Mexican merchants to trade more freely.

advances.name: Mining Boom
advances.text:
Industrial-scale silver extraction from the great mines of Guanajuato and Zacatecas generates wealth that flows across the globe, making New Spain the richest colony in the Americas.

Available in: Hacienda Grande

advances.name: Criollo Consciousness
advances.text: Mexican-born Spaniards develop a distinct identity, pride in their American homeland, and resentment of peninsular privilege, the intellectual foundation of the independence movement.

advances.name: Independence Movement
advances.text: From Hidalgo's Grito to Morelos's Congress of Chilpancingo to Guerrero's guerrilla campaigns, the independence movement forges a new national identity through a decade of revolutionary warfare.

event.title: The Cry of Dolores
event.text: In the early hours of September 16, 1810, in the small town of Dolores in the Bajio, Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla rings the church bell to summon his parishioners. What he proclaims that morning will echo through the centuries: death to bad government, death to the gachupines, long live the Virgin of Guadalupe. Within days, a ragtag army of tens of thousands (mestizos, indigenous peoples, mine workers, peasants) is marching on Guanajuato, then San Luis Potosi, then Mexico City itself. The insurgency will take eleven years, cost hundreds of thousands of lives, and produce a nation unlike any the world has seen: neither wholly Spanish nor wholly indigenous, but something entirely new.

options.text: A new nation is born from the people's courage.

advances.name: Guerrilla Tradition
advances.text: The insurgent guerrilleros, mestizo and indigenous fighters who waged irregular warfare against royalist forces, establish a Mexican military tradition of popular resistance that endures for generations.

advances.name: Plan de Iguala
advances.text: The Plan of the Three Guarantees unites insurgent republicans and royalist conservatives, creating a broad coalition that achieves independence through negotiation rather than conquest.

advances.name: Constitution of 1824
advances.text: Mexico's first republican constitution establishes a federal system modeled partly on the United States, with elected representatives, separation of powers, and sovereignty residing in the nation.

advances.name: Pulque Industry
advances.text:
The commercial cultivation of maguey and industrial production of pulque transforms an ancient sacred beverage into one of Mexico's most important domestic industries.

Available in: Hacienda Grande

advances.name: Reform of 1833
advances.text: Under Vice President Gomez Farias the first liberal reform is passed. Tithes and monastic vows lose the force of civil law, the Pontifical University is closed and public instruction is placed under the state.

event.title: The Reform of 1833
event.text: With President Santa Anna retired to his hacienda, Vice President Valentin Gomez Farias governs, and with Jose Maria Luis Mora at his side he carries the first liberal reform through Congress. The payment of tithes and the keeping of monastic vows are no longer enforced by civil law. The missions of the Californias are secularized, the Pontifical University is closed and a directorate of public instruction takes its place. The regular army is to be reduced and its fuero is questioned, while the states arm their civic militias. The bishops protest, and garrisons pronounce under the cry of religion and fueros. The reform can be pressed in the schools and the law, or the republic can be defended in arms.

options.text: The laws stand: the Church shall not rule the schools or the courts.

modifiers.name: Laws of 1833
modifiers.text: The tithe and the monastic vow are no longer enforced by civil law, the Pontifical University is closed and public instruction is placed under a directorate of the state. Congress legislates where the Church once ruled.

options.text: Arm the civic militia: the republic is defended by its citizens.

modifiers.name: Civic Militia
modifiers.text: Citizens of every state are enrolled in the civic militia to defend the republic and its laws. Armed by their own states, they are bound to the nation's cause and not to the generals of the regular army.

advances.name: Tribunal of the Acordada
advances.text: The judge of the Acordada and his mounted lieutenants ride the roads of the country against highwaymen. A bandit taken is tried and sentenced where he is caught, with no appeal to the courts of the capital.

advances.name: Mestizo Nation
advances.text: Mexico embraces mestizaje (the blending of indigenous, European, and African heritage) as the defining principle of national identity, creating a society that transcends the racial categories of the colonial era.

advances.name: Secularization of the Missions
advances.text: By the law of 1833 the missions of the Californias are taken from the friars. Their lands and herds pass to the state and to settlers, and the republic claims the patronage over the Church that the kings of Spain once held.

advances.name: Banco de Avio
advances.text: Founded in 1830 at the urging of Lucas Alaman, the Banco de Avio lends public money for machinery. Mechanized cotton mills are raised in Puebla, and the flooded silver mines of Real del Monte are drained with steam engines.

advances.name: Veracruz Trade
advances.text: The port of Veracruz, Mexico's gateway to the Atlantic and the Caribbean, becomes the hub of an expanding maritime commerce linking Mexican exports to global markets.

advances.name: Federalist Republic
advances.text: The federal system grants autonomy to Mexico's diverse states and regions, balancing central authority with local governance in a vast and heterogeneous nation.

destiny.name: Mexican Destiny
destiny.text: Mexico has been forged from the fires of revolution and the weight of colonial inheritance. Now it must choose its path: empire or republic, conquest or commerce, the sword or the silver peso.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: A Nation Takes Shape
event.text: The foundations of the new Mexico are laid. From the silver mines of the Bajio to the cocoa groves of the Gulf coast, from the ancient pyramids of Teotihuacan to the bustling markets of Oaxaca, this land holds the potential for greatness. The question is not whether Mexico will rise, but what form that rise will take.

destiny.name: Northern March
destiny.text: Push the frontier into the vast lands of Aridoamerica. Secure Culiacan and the northern silver country, and establish military dominance over the untamed frontier territories.

event.title: The Northern March
event.text: Mexican soldiers march north beyond the old presidio line, pushing into the vast silver country that the Chichimeca nations have long defended. Culiacan and the northern frontier are now under the Mexican eagle. With these territories secured, the treasury swells and the army grows stronger.

options.text: The frontier advances under the eagle and serpent.

destiny.name: Empire of Anahuac
destiny.text: Extend Mexican authority into the Sonoran desert and across the Rio Grande. Keep a great army in the field and carry imperial power to the edges of the continent.

conditions.text: Own Pitic, or a subject owns it
Own Yanaguana, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50

event.title: Empire of Anahuac
event.text: The Mexican Empire now stretches from the Sonoran desert to the banks of the Rio Grande. The question is how to govern this expanded domain. Some generals counsel an iron hand: swift military campaigns to crush any resistance and enforce central authority. Others look to the model of Iturbide's Plan de Iguala: a grand court that binds provincial elites through diplomacy, honors, and shared governance.

options.text: Rule with discipline: the empire needs an iron hand.

modifiers.name: Iron Hand
modifiers.text: Military discipline and swift campaigns enforce Mexican authority across the frontier. The army moves fast and strikes hard, though the constant warfare takes its toll on the nation.

options.text: Win hearts at court: loyalty freely given outlasts.

modifiers.name: Imperial Court
modifiers.text: The Mexican court, modeled on European monarchies, binds provincial elites through diplomacy, titles, and shared governance. A court of many nations, united under the eagle.

destiny.name: Continental Destiny
destiny.text: The Mexican Empire stretches from California to Guatemala, from the Gulf to the Pacific. A continental power rivaling any in the Old World, secured by the greatest army in the Americas.

conditions.text: Own Kumeyaay, or a subject owns it
Own Nacogdoches, or a subject owns it
Own Cuauhtemallan, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 75
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Continental Destiny
event.text: From the deserts of California to the jungles of Guatemala, the Mexican Empire has become the dominant power of the Western Hemisphere. This is the vision fulfilled: a great American empire that stands as the equal of any European power. The army that secured this territory must now be organized to defend it.

options.text: Build the greatest army in the Americas.

modifiers.name: Continental Army
modifiers.text: A massive standing army organized along modern lines, capable of sustaining operations across the entire Western Hemisphere.

options.text: Let diplomacy cement what the sword has won.

modifiers.name: American Dynasty
modifiers.text: The Mexican Empire commands respect through diplomatic prestige and dynastic connections, extending its influence across the hemisphere.

destiny.name: Silver Republic
destiny.text: The republic is built on the bedrock of silver. Guanajuato, whose Valenciana vein made it the richest silver camp of New Spain, is built up, the markets are widened, and the Mexican peso becomes the currency of the Americas.

event.title: The Silver Foundation
event.text: The republic has chosen a different path from the empire-builders. Rather than marshaling armies for conquest, Mexico turns inward to the wealth beneath its soil. The silver mines of Guanajuato, Zacatecas, and Taxco are the foundation of a prosperous republic.

options.text: The peso shall be the foundation of the republic.

destiny.name: Liberal Republic
destiny.text: The wealth of cocoa and silver is channelled into trade that serves the people. Veracruz, for three centuries the one licensed port of the viceroyalty, is opened and built up as the gate of free commerce.

conditions.text: The capital

event.title: The Liberal Republic
event.text: The commerce of the young republic is maturing. Merchant houses handle the flow of silver, cocoa merchants negotiate prices on the global market, and trade networks reach from the Gulf to the Pacific. Two visions emerge for Mexico's economic future.

options.text: The silver peso shall become the standard.

modifiers.name: Silver Standard
modifiers.text: The Mexican silver peso becomes the trusted standard of hemispheric trade, funding a growing merchant marine and naval tradition.

options.text: Build markets that serve the people, not the few.

modifiers.name: People's Market
modifiers.text: Cooperative banks and open markets channel the silver wealth to the common citizen. The army's maintenance suffers as resources flow to civil institutions.

destiny.name: Arsenal of Democracy
destiny.text: Mexico is transformed from an exporter of raw materials into an industrial republic. In Mexico City, where the Academy of San Carlos and the College of Mines once stood alone, a library is founded and schools are built, and a republic is shown to rival any monarchy in prosperity and progress.

conditions.text: We own Mexico City and it has a Library

event.title: Arsenal of Democracy
event.text: Mexico stands at the threshold of a new age. Learning has taken root in Mexico City, and the republic has the silver, the labor, and the institutions to industrialize. Schools rise across the nation, and a new generation of Mexican scientists and engineers prepares to transform raw materials into finished goods.

options.text: Build the schools: education is the future.

modifiers.name: Industrial Dawn
modifiers.text: Mexican factories produce goods for export across the Pacific and beyond. A new class of industrialists projects Mexican commercial power to distant shores.

options.text: An enlightened republic needs no empire.

modifiers.name: Enlightened Republic
modifiers.text: Mexico leads by example: an enlightened republic whose naval strength and diplomatic skill earn respect worldwide.

units.name: Soldados de Cuera
units.text: Leather-armored frontier dragoons armed with lance, shield, and musket. Born and raised on the northern frontier, these presidial cavalry are hardened by decades of warfare against Comanche and Apache raiders.

units.name: Insurgent Guerrilleros
units.text: Irregular fighters of the independence movement, mestizo peasants, mine workers, and indigenous warriors who wage guerrilla warfare in the mountains and barrancas of central Mexico.

units.name: Riders of the Acordada
units.text: Mounted lieutenants and commissioners of the Acordada, the tribunal of the roads. Fast light cavalry in small bands who hunt bandits across the countryside and are feared for their summary justice.

units.name: Manila Galleon
units.text: The nao de China, massive treasure ships that sail the Acapulco-Manila route, carrying Mexican silver westward and returning laden with Asian silk, spices, and porcelain. The largest and richest trade ships in the Pacific.

units.name: Corsario Guardacostas
units.text: Fast coastal patrol frigates that guard Mexico's extensive Gulf and Pacific coastlines against pirates, smugglers, and foreign encroachment.

buildings.name: Casa de Moneda
buildings.text: The Royal Mint strikes Mexican silver into pesos de ocho, the piece of eight, which circulate as the world's first global currency from the markets of Canton to the counting houses of Amsterdam.

buildings.name: Hacienda Grande
buildings.text: A great agricultural estate combining farming, ranching, and rural industry. The hacienda dominates the Mexican countryside, providing food and raw materials while employing hundreds of workers bound by debt peonage.

where.text: Silver is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Presidio Fronterizo
buildings.text: A fortified frontier garrison manned by professional soldiers. The presidio defends settled territory against indigenous raiders and serves as the nucleus of civilization on the northern frontier.

buildings.name: Cochineal Nopalry
buildings.text: Rows of nopal cactus seeded with the cochineal insect, tended by the households of the dye country and visited by the grana merchants. The dried insect is the world's most expensive dye, prized for the robes of European monarchs and Catholic cardinals, and the dye harvest of the land grows with the plantings.

buildings.name: Colegio Real
buildings.text: A royal college where both Spanish and indigenous elites are educated in theology, law, and the liberal arts, creating a distinctively Mexican intellectual tradition.

buildings.name: Baroque Cathedral
buildings.text: A magnificent Churrigueresque cathedral in the ultra-ornate Mexican Baroque style, blending Spanish ecclesiastical architecture with indigenous artistic motifs in a dazzling expression of mestizo cultural identity.

buildings.name: Palacio Imperial
buildings.text: The seat of the Mexican Emperor, a grand palace befitting a continental power. From here, the empire is administered and the destiny of the Americas is shaped.

buildings.name: Escuela Nacional
buildings.text: A national preparatory school that transforms Mexican youth into informed citizens, embodying the republic's commitment to universal education and scientific progress.

list.name: Plan de Iguala
list.text: Iturbide's Three Guarantees of 24 February 1821 (Religion, Independence, Union) gave the new Mexican state its only widely-accepted founding doctrine, bridging peninsular royalists, criollo liberals, and casta troops under the Catholic-monarchical-criollo banner of the Trigarante army. Sustained, it binds a racially heterogeneous nation under shared symbols. Neglected, the consensus fractures along the very fault lines it had papered over.

list.name: Patronato Eclesiastico
list.text: Inherited from the Spanish Bourbons, the Real Patronato gives the Mexican state the right to nominate bishops, collect tithes, and try clerics in church courts under the fuero eclesiastico. The church returns the favour by lending capital at favourable rates and disciplining rural parishes, but Jose Maria Luis Mora and the liberals from 1833 onward will demand the fueros' abolition as the price of a modern republic.

conditions.text: Catholicism religion

list.name: Sistema de Caudillos
list.text: Mexican politics from Iturbide's 1822 coronation through Santa Anna's first presidency in 1833 ran on regional military strongmen who raised personal armies, issued pronunciamientos, and rotated through the National Palace at gunpoint. The caudillo system delivers light cavalry across the Bajio in days and levies from local clientele, and delivers presidential instability on the same schedule.

list.name: Hacienda Latifundia
list.text: The great rural estate, descended from the colonial encomienda and consolidated under the Bourbon reforms, dominates Mexican agriculture from the central plateau to Yucatan. Hacendados hold debt-peons (peones acasillados) bound to the tienda de raya, supply urban grain markets, and pay wages in scrip. The system feeds the cities and bankrolls the landed aristocracy at the cost of permanent rural debt-bondage and stagnant yields.

list.name: Republicas de Indios
list.text: A colonial institution the 1821 republic formally abolished yet preserved in practice for decades: the segregated indigenous community, governed by elected alcaldes and gobernadores, paying communal tribute, and holding inalienable village lands (tierras comunales) outside the Spanish-American legal order. The shell protects Mexico's indigenous majority, but liberals already press to break up the comunales and put them on the open market.

list.name: Siete Leyes y Departamentos
list.text: The Centralist Republic of 1836 dissolved the federal states of the 1824 Constitution into appointive Departamentos under presidentially-named governors and property-qualified Juntas. A Supremo Poder Conservador, drawn from the Bourbon cameralist tradition, gained the power to veto Congress and depose the president. The machinery suppressed regional rebellion at the price of provoking it: Zacatecas in 1835 and Texas in 1836 were the warning.
